title: Sampati
hook: a hungry old vulture hears his brother's name

segments.voice: Yesterday: Svayamprabha behind them, and a line of monkeys on the shore, sitting down to fast, talking about Jatayu. Did you say an urge to quit out loud? Day five hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `A LINE OF MONKEYS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Out of a cave on the hillside comes an enormous old bird. He has no wings to speak of; what's left of them is burned. He drags himself out onto the rocks and looks down at a beach covered with monkeys, all sitting perfectly still. And he says to himself, more or less: what luck. A meal, lined up and waiting to die. As each one goes, I'll eat him. The monkeys hear him. Nobody on that beach is sitting quite so still anymore.
screen: `AN OLD BIRD ON THE ROCKS.` → `BURNED WINGS.` → `WHAT LUCK: A MEAL.`

segments.voice: The monkeys are terrified. Angada, already in despair, says it aloud to Hanuman: look, death has come for us in the shape of a bird. And then he goes on lamenting, and he names Jatayu again. Even Jatayu, he says, gave his life for Rama. We're dying for Rama too. The old bird freezes. Who said Jatayu? he calls down. Who is speaking of my brother? His voice changes from a hunter's to family's. I haven't heard that name in so long. Tell me: is Jatayu dead? How did it happen? The hunter has become a mourner. His name is Sampati, he tells them, and Jatayu was his younger brother. He asks them to help him down from the hill, and the monkeys, still uneasy, do. Angada tells him the whole story: Rama's exile, Sita taken, Jatayu's fight with Ravana in the sky, his death, and the funeral Rama gave him. Sampati grieves for his brother right there on the beach. Watch how the story travels. Jatayu's death, which looked like a defeat months ago in the story, now saves the whole southern party. Because they spoke his name, the bird who meant to eat them asks them to tell him more. In this poem, nothing given for Rama seems to go to waste. Tomorrow Sampati tells his own story, and how he lost his wings.
screen: `ANGADA NAMES JATAYU.` · `WHO SPEAKS OF MY BROTHER?` · `SAMPATI GRIEVES ON THE BEACH.` · `NOTHING GIVEN GOES TO WASTE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a name that matters to you: someone you've lost touch with, or lost. Say it silently. Breathe in, and notice what happens in your chest when you do. Breathe out, and let the name stay there, warm. Sometimes just saying a name brings someone closer. Stay with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Sampati. The wingless old vulture who comes for a meal, hears his brother's name, and becomes family.
Your line: who speaks of my brother. Today, mention someone you love and miss in conversation. Say their name aloud. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sampati and Jatayu are often told about together in Ramayana storytelling, as two brothers who both serve Rama: one by fighting Ravana, one by seeing where he went.

match.prompt: the bird on the hill — tap the pairs.

myth: Sampati is happy to help from the start
he first sees the monkeys as a meal.
hearing Jatayu's name changes Sampati's whole manner
he calls down asking who speaks of his brother.
Sampati already knew Jatayu had died
he learns it from the monkeys and grieves.

fork.setup: you're Sampati, old and hungry, looking at a line of monkeys who've sat down to die. then you hear your brother's name. what do you do?
options: call down and ask who is speaking of your brother.
fork.reveal: Sampati asks about Jatayu, and the monkeys help him down and tell him the whole story.

original.note: Sanskrit sampāti: the elder brother of Jatayu, a great vulture.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monster shows up to eat the monkeys.
what it means: it's Jatayu's brother, and the name turns hunger into grief.
what a scholar hears: Kishkindha 56 has Sampati see the monkeys as food and Angada's lament naming Jatayu; Kishkindha 57 has Sampati's questions.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 56–57 (Sampati appears; Angada's lament; Sampati asks about Jatayu)
